**The hard rules, the working style and the architecture rules.** This file is attached to
every session, so it holds only what is worth paying for on every turn.

**New to this project? Read `START-HERE.md` first** — one page, ten minutes, and it names the current state, the traps, and which of the other documents to open and when. Then come back here.

Three companions carry what used to be here, and none of them is auto-attached:
**`DECISIONS.md`** is why every settled choice is the way it is, **`LESSONS.md`** is every
mistake already paid for once, and **`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md`** is current mechanics, structure
and commands.

---

## The bug shapes that have cost the most

**Read this before debugging anything.** Every one of these got past a clean build at `/W4` *and* a clean soak, and every one was found by the user or by a hand audit, never by a tool. What is here is enough to *recognise* one; **`LESSONS.md` has the full story of each**, and the fix is usually a `constexpr` assert rather than care.

1. **A value derived somewhere other than the one table that owns it.** This is the root of most of the rest. It compiles, it looks plausible, it is subtly wrong. **When you widen what something can be, grep for the old literals** — nothing changed type, so the compiler cannot help. **And grep any new enumerator's name before you write it**: `RedstoneLampLit` and three froglights were both added a second time, five milestones apart, because three thousand ids in, "does this already exist?" feels like a question you know the answer to.
2. **Widening a family predicate kills every early-out already sitting behind it.** `isFurnace` grew to cover smokers and silently turned eight `case` labels in `blockName` into dead code. **Grep every existing caller, not just the new one.** **The remedy, when the new case needs its own behaviour: add a flag beside the old one rather than widening it.** Campfire contact damage was built exactly this way — `Player.cpp` declares `inCampfire` next to `inFire`, fills it in the same occupied-block scan and reads it in **one** branch, because `inFire` has **three** readers (an armour-reduced branch, a `burningSeconds` branch and a `!inLava && !inFire` guard) and widening it would have silently changed all three. **Count the readers of a predicate before you widen it; if the new case does not want all of them, it wants its own variable** — and whether it should inherit the *other* behaviours is a separate question to answer on its own evidence, not by sharing a name.
3. **A number ported into a field measured in a different unit.** It compiles, it validates, and the system around it works perfectly. **Write down what a ported number is measured against.**
4. **A predicate written as "equals the empty case" where a general test already exists.** Water drew its surface where `ahead == Air`, so a lily pad beside it erased the surface; `occludesFace` was one line away. **The symptom names the newest arrival, never the old rule.**
5. **A derivation applied to one of a pair and not the other.** `flipV` was read off the face tables and `flipU` was not, mirroring every shaped block in the game for four milestones. **Derive both from the same table and write the `constexpr` assert.**
6. **A blended fragment still writes depth.** Anything transparent stamps its distance and rejects whatever is drawn *later* behind it — three separate bugs in two days. **Ask it of any HUD geometry that overlaps.**
7. **A fixed simulation step needs render interpolation.** **Never raise the tick rate to fix smoothness**; every published constant is per tick and four asserts depend on it. Keep the previous tick and blend in the renderer.
8. **A format-version migration promises that old *damage* stays, not just old data.** **When a version bump changes nothing, read the bytes on disk before doubting the fix.**
9. **A standard formula written from memory can come out inverted, and consuming it as a *ratio* hides that.** **Print a curve you did not derive on the spot at three known points before trusting it.**
10. **A `default:` that returns a real value hides every missing entry — and there is usually more than one `default:`.** A per-run catch-all is not a shortcut, it is a second place for the identical bug. **Make the inner one fall through to the outer rule.** **A search that returns its first match is the same bug in disguise, and it defeats asserts rather than callers.** `attributeDescriptions()` declares 5 rows and assigns them by index, so an unwritten row is not absent — it is `location = 0, VK_FORMAT_UNDEFINED`, a *duplicate* of the real location 0. Every one of the five `static_assert`s reaches it through `vertexAttributeAt`, which **finds the genuine row first and never sees the duplicate**, so all five pass on a green build while the pipeline hands the undefined format straight to `pVertexInputState`. **When an accessor searches, ask what it does with a second match** — and prefer asserting on the array directly over asserting through the finder.
11. **A `static_assert` comparing one side of a derivation against itself proves nothing.** Eleven of them passed while pointing at the wrong texture. **Assert the whole expression the real reader evaluates, base and all.** **And the sharper form, 2026-08-19: ask where the assert's expected value CAME FROM.** Copper oxidised **four times too slowly** and *all three* of its asserts passed — not because they compared a thing to itself, but because **assert and implementation were both transcribed from the same wrong reading of the reference.** An assert is only evidence if its number has a **different provenance** from the code's; if the answer is "the same place", it is decoration wearing a proof's clothes. The replacement derives its values from the reference's own worked example and carries a negative twin.
12. **Rectangles guessed out of an image instead of read from the model that names them.** One bed, four playtest rounds, one mistake — and then twenty more blocks and every dropped item. The reference's `models/block/*.json` states every box, every face's `uv` rect and which texture it uses. **When a block is more than a cube, open its JSON first**, and **run `tools/check-models.ps1`**, which measures every block that has a model against it in one command — **2629 of them today, 0 disagreeing**, plus a box count over 359 `Model` blocks and 95 face rectangles read straight out of `Block.hpp`. Where the reference has no model — a bell body is a block entity — say so and measure the art, rather than guessing and calling it the reference. **And when you improve a checker, expect its fault count to go up and do not read that as having broken something**: this tool went 1792/0, then 2539/**275**, then 2629/0 in a single session, and the 275 appeared because it stopped comparing union extents alone, which had been passing a flower pot whose two X walls carried the lid's rect and a scaffolding missing its four top rails.
13. **A block is drawn in four places, and fixing the world fixes one of them.** The mesher, the slot picture, the dropped entity and the thrown entity. Every non-flat block item was dropped as a single spinning cube for twenty milestones because nobody threw one on the floor. **When you change how a block looks, ask where else it is drawn** — and give the answer one owner rather than four. **Paid a third and fourth time on 2026-08-11**, both found by play and both invisible from the world: the drop handed one side layer to all four side quads, so a sticky piston wore its front right round, and the icon painted the side layer on the lid of every model-shaped block, so an end portal frame lost its eye socket. **The three paths differ in how many face directions they can be told** — the mesher one per face, the icon two, the drop four — and any that settles for a single answer is wrong for every block whose faces differ.

14. **A rule that exists, is correct, and is commented — in only one of the two places that need it.** Lava's pooling test was water's rule minus the single clause that made water right, so a poured column shelved sideways at every level. The player fell through not-yet-loaded chunks and was buried when they arrived, for twenty milestones, while creatures — guarded against precisely that since the day they were written, with the reason spelled out in their own comment — never did. **Neither is a missing rule you could grep for; both are a rule that did not travel.** When you write a guard, a fallback or an exception, ask what else does the same thing, and put the answer in one function both call.

15. **A complete feature sitting one predicate, one call site or one enumerator short of being reachable at all.** Seven of these in a single audit pass on 2026-08-17: brewing unreachable because `isInteractive` never named the stand, armour inert because `armourDefence` had zero callers, three status-effect helpers likewise, sixteen sound events staged and never triggered, rail curves impossible because placement emits two of the ten shapes, the random-tick sampler filtered to crops alone. **All seven were closed by 2026-08-19, and the shape produced an eighth that lasted thirty-two minutes** — bees: at 09:59 nests generated, bees pollinated, shearing a full hive was written and commented as the game's only source of honeycomb, and **nothing consumed `Creatures::takePollinated`**, so no hive filled; at 10:23 the drain landed. **Closing every instance does not retire the shape; expect the next one.** **And a negative claim, correctly measured with a control, went stale in half an hour** — so date every "nothing calls this" and **re-read the date before acting on it**, because with several agents writing at once the falsifier you named may already have fired. **Every one built clean, validated clean, and did nothing** — there is no dead-code warning for a table nobody reads. **Grep a new function's own name for call sites before believing the feature works**, and count the enumerators the *writer* can emit against the ones the reader handles. **But that grep has a false-positive class that produced four near-regressions in one evening: a value routed through a struct, a table or an index cast is invisible to a call-site sweep** — forty names in `Creature.cpp` sit in a behaviour table without parentheses, sixteen `CreatureKind` enumerators are written by an index cast, and `familyRoughness` was reported dead while feeding the GPU through a packed row. **Search the bare name too, and follow the data as well as the calls.** **Two more ways this class hides, both found on 2026-08-19.** **The sweep term that beats "no caller" is the house phrase itself — `"one call site short"` — because the author who fears a bug names it**; sweep its neighbours too (`nothing reads`, `built but`, `dormant`, `unreachable`). **And the instance no negative-word search can ever reach is a spec written in the IMPERATIVE**: *"for each cell, read the block… write `beeHomeAtLevel(id, level + 1)`"* is **a negative claim containing no negative words** — every sentence true, none of them saying the work is still owed — so *not / never / missing / TODO* all miss it, a reader honours it, and now two writers raise one honey level. **Sweep for instruction-shaped comments — "write", "add", "the fix is", "needs a", "should call" — and for each, ask whether it has already been done.** It is a header and comment problem rather than a document one: a gap list states gaps as facts, so it rots in the findable direction. **And run the sweep with a graded control** — a name you know is live *and* a name you invent that cannot exist — because "0 hits" from a broken query looks exactly like "0 hits" from a real absence.

16. **A comment that is wrong while the code is right - and it is the most dangerous kind, because every review passes.** Measured at **4 false claims in 16 checkable ones in a single file**, and not one of them was a wrong line number. Three would have made a careful reader break working code: one recommended widening `kSpawnEggLayers`, the exact edit its own counter-argument thirty-five lines below forbids because those item ids sit in saved inventories on disk; one marked a function "No caller" when a *gameplay* caller had appeared after the note was written about the *display* side; one cited the wrong `RESEARCH.md` line, so verifying suffocation damage would lead you to quadruple it. Nothing in this project catches one - not the compiler, not a sweep, not a soak - and a confident comment in this codebase's voice is trusted precisely because the rest have earned it. **Rank them by what a reader would *do*, and fix in that order**: a comment arguing for a breaking edit, then one claiming a guard that does not exist, then one calling a load-bearing thing redundant, and only last a wrong line number. **Negative claims rot fastest**, because the world only has to move once - so date "nothing calls this" and name what would make it false. **The asymmetry is measured, not felt: across three sweeps on 2026-08-19 a claim that something was ABSENT was wrong five times in eight, then six in six, then seven more — and never once in the other direction.** Nothing all day claimed a thing existed that did not. It is structural: something gets built and nothing revisits the note saying it was missing, so **"X is missing" is the least reliable sentence in this repository and "X is broken" is far sounder.** Weight them differently, **and fix the comment as part of closing the gap** — a negative claim in a header outlives every ledger entry, because the next reader has the file and not the ledger. **A dated claim with a named falsifier is a different kind of object from a claim**: two of these were caught going stale within half an hour of being written, by their own falsifiers, and re-reading a page of them costs five minutes.

**Two that are about method rather than code, and they are worth as much:**

- **Measure before optimising, and the answer will not be one of the three you would have guessed.** The plan was to drop distant plants (13.7% of geometry, worth 4.3%); a throwaway probe binning triangles *by height band* found 65% of all geometry sealed inside rock where nothing can see it, and dropping unlit distant faces was worth four times the headline feature. **Write the probe before writing the optimisation, then delete it.** And the general form, which this project has now paid for four more times in one round: **on any table-shaped question, the probe is the first move rather than the last.** The furnace duplicating every input stack, 612 blocks silently dropped from the fuel table, every shaped block's drop mirrored for four milestones, eight beehives demoted from wood to rock — all four sat in code that had been read, twice over in a round convened to read it, and all four fell out of a thirty-line probe in minutes. **Reading finds what looks wrong; a wrong row looks exactly like a right one, and there are three thousand of them.** Dumping every id before and after an edit is also what makes a change *safe* rather than merely correct — it turns "I think this only affects carpets" into "16 removed, 0 added, 0 retimed".
- **Before writing the third near-identical row, ask what the rows actually differ by.** If the answer is one field, that field is the table. `ShapedFamily` carries a parent block and `shapedParent` forwards six answers — which is how **640 blocks arrived in one afternoon with no new art and no new rows**, after twenty milestones of having exactly one stair type because a second one meant seven edits in seven files. **The same question applies to a constant that another file must agree with, and there the answer is a ladder — 2026-08-19.** *Derive one side from the other* so the coupling cannot break (`kModelSweepStride = (kBlockIdCount + 7) / 8` needs no comment, no assert and no maintenance, because the stride *is* the count); failing that, *a `constexpr` assert sited where the breaking edit happens*; and only then *a comment*, which rots — one such comment listed three blockers when one was real and cited a line that moved twice in an evening. **A hand-written constant that must match another file is a row that differs by one field.** **The cleanest demonstration is one file pair holding both answers: `Renderer.cpp`'s binding array needs *nothing*, because each constant is its predecessor + 1 and the size derives from the last, so a gap is not expressible — while the vertex-attribute array beside it needs an assert purely because its `5` is a hand-written literal. **⚠️ But do not read that as "a derived size needs nothing" — that holds only for the *run* shape, where each constant is its predecessor + 1 so a gap cannot be expressed.** Two properties are involved and **derivation fixes only one of them**: declared size versus the enum is dissolved by deriving it, but **literal rows versus declared size is not**, because `std::array<T, DerivedN> x{{...}}` still zero-fills a short initialiser. `Loot.hpp`'s `kTables` is sized `static_cast<std::size_t>(TableId::Count)` — as derived as it gets, and its own note records that this correctly *replaced* a now-tautological `static_assert` — **yet nothing there ever covered a missing row.** **So run the declared-versus-literal check even on tables whose size is derived.** **And bound the first rung honestly: deriving a column that is only coincidentally equal is a fiction, and a fiction that makes a check look derived is worse than an honest assert** — a shadow-quality table whose top row happens to equal `kMaxCascades` while the rest read 0, 2 and 3 was correctly left with an assert sited under the table instead.** **And the strongest way to derive is to make the compiler hold the constraint: a raw array decays to a pointer, and a pointer carries no bound** — `CreatureKind species[4]` passed as `CreatureKind* out` was two unlinked literal `4`s, and `out[4]` would have been a silent write past the end with no diagnostic possible. Taking `CreatureKind (&out)[kMaxPenSpecies]` puts the bound **in the function's type**, where caller and callee cannot disagree. **If you pass a raw array to a function, ask whether a reference-to-array would let the compiler check it for you.** **What decides between the last two rungs: where a coupling fails LOUDLY prefer the assert, and where it fails SILENTLY the comment is the only instrument that exists** — restoring powder snow's collision box makes its suffocation clause the only thing between the player and a two-second death *and* makes freezing unreachable, both with a green build, so no assert can catch either. **Site the warning in the file whose edit would BREAK it, not in the file that suffers** — the reader about to break something is the one who must be told, and neither owner can otherwise see the coupling. **Cite symbolically, date it, name the falsifier, and give a search rather than a list**: a list rots, a search does not, and one such comment named three blockers when one was real while its line number moved twice in a single evening.
- **Before you write a probe, make a count, or claim something does not exist, read `MEASURING.md`.** It was this bullet until 2026-08-19, when it reached 12,199 characters — 20% of a file attached to every session, paid for on every turn whether or not anyone was measuring anything. Nothing was dropped in the move. **What must stay resident, because it decides whether to open that file at all:** ⓪ **is this token the only way the concept could be spelled?** — no control can answer it, and it is the leg that kills claims (`Enum::Name` is a prefix of `Enum::NameFirst`; ids get minted by helpers, index casts and packed rows; a field name can belong to two structs). **The one-question diagnostic:** *if this control came out the other way, would the CLAIM be false, or the INSTRUMENT broken?* — first is a claim control, second an instrument control, **neither means vacuous**. **A measurement is a fact with a timestamp: record "already fixed", never "never broken", and check mtime against a report before concluding the report was wrong.** **`std::array` silently zero-fills a short initialiser** — declared size vs literal row count, and run it even where the size is derived. **Print the corpus size, not just the subject count.** **A STOP is held to a higher bar than a FIX, because a stop is self-sealing** — and when you must choose a direction to fail in, **choose false-alarm.**

## If you are a new session, read this box first

Eight things that will otherwise cost the user time they have already paid once.

0. **⚠️ THE TREE HAS NOT COMPILED SINCE 2026-08-19.** A 27-agent correctness round ran for five hours under a hardware throttle — no `cmake`, no `cl`, no `glslc` — and landed **64 files, +7,537 / −1,045, none of it built.** That was correct and instructed, but it means **an `.obj` proves its TU as of its own timestamp, not today**, and eleven-plus widely-included headers were rewritten after the newest one. **Before anything else, ask whether the hardware is clear and get a build.** The ranked aims are in the session workspace at `files/46-build-plan-round2.md`, and its most useful part is the list of failures that will be **misread** — several asserts will fire in a way that looks like the fix broke them when it is really the assert doing its job. **`audit.md` §A0 is the same list in the repository.**

1. **Bedrock Edition is the reference, not Java.** Direct instruction 2026-08-03. Where they differ — attack cooldown, hitboxes, creeper damage, entity cramming, mob caps, despawning — Bedrock wins. `RESEARCH.md` marks Java values `[JE]` throughout.
2. **Never commit to Git.** Not once, not "to be tidy", not while wrapping up a milestone. Write files and leave them uncommitted.
3. **The user is the playtester and has said so three times, the last in capitals.** Anything needing aim, a held button, or a judgement about feel goes to them. **Two failed screenshot-harness attempts is the signal to stop**, restore `settings.cfg` and `saves/*/player.dat`, hand over the build, and say what to look at.
4. **Building a creature model has a written procedure and skipping it is why the last three looked wrong.** `TEXTURING.md` "Reading a net you have never seen before" — alpha runs before island detection, missing rects as placement clues, colour where arithmetic ties, a **shared-extent scan before rendering**, then two renders and the eye. Budget is two renders; a third means the *pose* is wrong, not the numbers.
5. **Subagents must be launched with `model: "Claude Opus 5 (copilot)"`.** Omitting the parameter silently gets a small default and the research comes back thin.
6. **"Both presets clean, zero validation errors" proves almost nothing.** It proves it does not crash, and says nothing about per-block tables, icons, screen state, item conservation or whether a model is *right*. Three separate sweeps found five, then ten, then seven real bugs in code that had already passed exactly that bar. **A temporary startup probe logging `constexpr` per-block functions checks the lot in one run** — and where both sides are `constexpr`, **a `static_assert` can never rot**, which is what `foodTablesAgree()` is.
7. **A worldgen fix that tests clean can still be plainly broken on screen, because the world you are looking at was loaded rather than generated.** Water flow calls `setBlock`, which flags a chunk modified, so merely standing near an ocean writes chunks to disk. **Check `saves/`, and bump `kChunkFormatVersion` — that is what it is for.**

## Critical — Read First

- **Never run `git commit`, `git push`, or any history-rewriting command unless explicitly asked.** Direct user correction, 2026-07-30: _"undo those commits. who told you to commit. keep changes that's fine, no committing."_ Three commits had been created unprompted while wrapping up Milestone 1, on the reasoning that the user had asked for "Git-friendly incremental changes" — that phrase describes how changes should be *shaped* (small, reviewable, not giant rewrites), **not** permission to run Git for them. Write files, leave them uncommitted, and let the user decide when and what to commit. `git init` and `.gitignore` were fine; the commits were not.
- **Ship something playable at every milestone, and treat the user as the primary QA resource.** Direct user instruction, 2026-07-30: _"the best thing for the game is to get playability on early so that i can 'play' the game and report findings back to you. i am the most valuable bug finding resource you can have."_ `TIMELINE.md` was reordered because of this — first playability moved from M9 to M7, textures and chunk streaming were pushed *after* walking and block-breaking. A milestone that produces nothing runnable is too big; split it. When the user reports a bug, **default to "this is real and I haven't found it yet,"** not to explaining why the code looks fine.

  The evidence is old and consistent: three of four M3 bugs and both M7 bugs were found by playing, not by review, and none produced a warning or a validation error.
- **When the user names a milestone, build it. Splitting it is my job, not a question to hand back.** Direct correction, 2026-08-01: _"exactly what part of 'start m20' did you not understand? my word is absolute authority and you have wasted hours of my time... you could've autonomously seen how big m20 is and split it up into subparts on your own and then accomplished it."_ I was told to do M20, correctly worked out it needed splitting into M20a, wrote that down as a recommendation — and then did not do it. **Knowing the answer and stopping is worse than getting it wrong.** Bugs are an expected cost of development and the user says so plainly; *not starting* is not. Time spent deliberating while they are away is time taken directly from them. Being away is exactly when long autonomous work should happen, not when it should pause.
- **The long, highly detailed vision prompts were written by another AI, not by the user.** Disclosed 2026-07-30: _"the bigger and more detailed prompts i gave weren't me, they were another ai helping me get my stuff sorted, so take what it says with a grain of salt."_ Those feature lists are a **statement of ambition and a menu of options, not a specification**. Do not treat any bullet in them as a commitment, do not implement something merely because it is listed, and where they conflict with the user's own plain-language wishes, **the user wins**. Their short, direct messages are the authoritative signal.

  **This was violated for fifteen milestones.** The vision documents' "everything must be original" rule was carried into `TIMELINE.md` as a hard requirement and enforced until the user objected — costing them a push-back they should never have had to make. When something in the plan cannot be traced to the user, **say so and ask**, rather than defending it.

  Audited 2026-07-31. **Confirmed by the user directly:** the graphics ambition is real — ray tracing, volumetric clouds, the modern renderer — delivered as **settings rather than requirements** (a `Video` tab with quality toggles). The 35-milestone structure is wanted. Do not re-question either. **Ray tracing itself is parked**, agreed 2026-08-17: _"i agree ray tracing is a long way out."_ M30 stays on the list, untouched.
- **Stop at milestone boundaries.** The user explicitly asked (2026-07-30) that work stop at the end of each milestone and wait for instruction. Do not roll straight from "the window renders" into "now let's add chunks." Finishing early and asking is correct behavior here, not laziness.
- **The user is an experienced vibe coder but NOT an experienced C++/graphics-engine programmer.** They understand concepts when explained simply. Do not assume familiarity with low-level graphics or systems terminology.
- **Use the real term, then immediately explain it in plain English.** Direct user instruction, 2026-07-30: _"remember i'm just a vibe coder i don't understand all this complex terminology so use the terminology, then explain it in simple human terms so i learn over time."_ This is a learning-over-time request, not a request to dumb things down — do not silently substitute vague language for the correct word, and do not drop the plain-English half either.
- **Do not build ahead of the current milestone.** No voxel terrain, physics, ray tracing, procedural generation, PBR, weather, or job systems until explicitly asked. The long-term ambition is real, but building toward it speculatively is the fastest way to a codebase nobody can finish. `TIMELINE.md` records the intended order and why.
- **Multiplayer is permanently cut, not deferred.** User decision, 2026-07-30: _"no multiplayer btw."_ This is a **design freedom, not a limitation** — treat single-player as a licence to avoid client/server splits, server-authoritative simulation, replication hooks, and determinism constraints that exist only to serve netcode. Do not add abstractions "in case multiplayer happens later." An earlier draft of the vision listed multiplayer as long-term; that was explicitly overridden.
- **The overworld is the whole game. The Nether and The End are out of scope and are deliberately not on the timeline.** Ruling 2026-08-17: _"our main focus is limited to the overworld, not nether or end, those are far far far away on the timeline (doesn't exist on timeline, leave it like that) because overworld itself has a lotta work waiting for us."_ Their absence from `TIMELINE.md` is the decision, not an oversight — **do not plan, research or build a portal, a second dimension or a single Nether block**, and a "general" dimension stack is not foresight. Where an overworld system wants an ingredient that only exists over there — blaze powder for brewing — **note it in one line and drop it**.
- **This machine's Windows account is a standard user, not an administrator.** See "The Machine" below. Never ask the user to type a password or PIN into anything the model can read.
- **Windows PowerShell 5.1 only. Never use `&&`** — chain with `;`. **Never send multi-line scripts to the terminal** (see Lessons).
- **Never write a source file with `Out-File`, `>` or `Set-Content` — they add a BOM, and this rule has now been broken four times.** Use `[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($p, $s, [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false))` or `AppendAllText`, for every edit including one-line ones; there is no size at which the redirect is safe. **Then run `tools/check-ascii.ps1 -Path <file>`, one path per call** — it takes under a second and reports bytes, BOM, NUL, non-ASCII and U+FFFD in one line. **Read that line rather than the exit code**, because a multi-path `powershell -File` invocation joins the paths into a single string and prints a green line for a file it never opened, where the only tell is a byte count of 0. As of 2026-08-19 07:30 the code is trustworthy on its own — 1 for a missing path *or* real damage, 0 only when it checked and found nothing — but it exited 0 on a BOM earlier that same day, so confirm rather than assume. It existed for both of the 2026-08-18 breakages and neither agent ran it, which is why this is here rather than only in `LESSONS.md`: writing the rule down has already failed twice. **And a batch of edits can land partly, which under a no-build throttle is the likeliest way anyone here ships a broken tree.** Three edits went out together, the two `.cpp` ones landed and the `.hpp` one failed on a bad anchor, leaving **2 uses and 0 definitions** — a guaranteed compile error in a tree nobody could compile to find it. **When one edit defines what another consumes, land the definition first and re-read the file rather than trusting the batch's success report**, because the compiler that normally catches this in seconds may be hours away. **In markdown the same shape is a heading cited by a section that landed while the heading did not** — check the anchors, not the tool's report. **For markdown use `tools/check-encoding.ps1` instead** — documents carry intentional non-ASCII and `check-ascii` reports it as damage. **And `WriteAllText` of a here-string writes bare LF, because the here-string carries whatever ending the transport gave it — so the method this bullet mandates is also the one that mixed four files on 2026-08-19, including all 4,725 lines of `GAPS.md`.** The repository is CRLF. Normalise first — ``$s = $s -replace "`r`n|`r|`n", "`r`n"``, three alternations and **backticks not backslashes**, because `"\r\n"` inserts four literal characters and destroys every ending — or use the `edit` tool, which is safe on a pure-CRLF file like every file in this tree — though not a repair for a mixed one, because it infers its convention from the span it replaces. A mixed file then *silently shrinks* any search whose newline is a literal `\n`, and misses rather than failing loudly.
- **This is not being built inside Unity, Unreal, or Godot, and that is not up for casual reconsideration.** The whole point is a custom engine. If a task feels like it "would be easier in Unreal," that is expected and not a signal to switch.
- **Do not add a dependency unless the current milestone actually needs it.** Every dependency must be justifiable in one sentence at the moment it is added, not "we'll want it eventually."
- **Threading landed at M12 and is confined to generation and meshing.** Everything else is main-thread by design, and the three purity rules in "Architecture Rules" are what keep it that way. Do not widen it without a measurement saying the serial part is the problem.

## The User and Working Style

The three big ones — vibe coder not a C++ programmer, term-then-plain-English, playtester — are in "Critical" above. What is not there:

- Thinks in terms of outcomes and feel ("large procedural worlds," "high-quality graphics"), not APIs. Translate that into technical plans rather than asking them to specify the technical plan. Do the low-level reasoning and stack-trace interpretation yourself.
- Wants to **understand**, not just receive working code. Before introducing a new library, tool or concept: what it is, why we need it _now_, what happens without it. A few sentences — the instruction was explicitly "do not drown me in theory."
- Prefers that missing tools be **installed**, not merely reported as missing. Only escalate to "you need to do this manually" when there is a genuine hard blocker (admin rights, a license click, a hardware limitation), and even then, automate everything on either side of the blocker.
- Wants verification, not assumption. "It should work now" is not acceptable — build it and run it.
- Expects Git-friendly incremental change. No giant speculative rewrites.

## The Machine (2026-07-30)

Facts about this specific development machine that have already cost time to discover:

- **The Windows user account `arnav` is a standard (non-administrator) user.** The local Administrators group contains `Administrator`, `haris`, and `sneha`. The user knows the `haris` PIN.
- **Consequence:** anything that installs into `C:\Program Files` or writes machine-wide registry keys cannot be installed silently by the agent. The working pattern that succeeded: the agent downloads the official installer, then launches it with `Start-Process -Verb RunAs`, and **the user completes Windows' own credential prompt themselves.** The PIN is never typed into, read by, or routed through the model. Reuse this pattern; do not invent alternatives.
- **User-scope installs are strongly preferred where they exist.** CMake and Ninja were installed as plain extracted archives under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\` with the user `Path` environment variable updated — no admin needed, trivially upgradable, and nothing to uninstall. Prefer this for any future standalone tool.
- **Hardware is not the bottleneck.** Intel Core Ultra 7 155H (16 cores / 22 threads), NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop GPU plus an Intel Arc integrated GPU, Windows 11. The RTX 4070 supports hardware ray tracing, so the long-term ray-tracing ambition is realistic on this machine — but see "Two GPUs" in `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md`, because *which* GPU Vulkan picks is a real decision, not an accident.
- **The Vulkan runtime was already present before any SDK was installed** (`C:\Windows\System32\vulkan-1.dll`, shipped by the GPU drivers). Do not confuse "Vulkan runs on this machine" with "the Vulkan SDK is installed" — they are separate things and only the second one gives us validation layers and a shader compiler.

## Architecture Rules

- **This is openly a game in Minecraft's tradition, and following it closely is the point.** Direct user correction, 2026-07-31: _"do you know how difficult that is? i would have to spend weeks coming up with an entire new mechanic... this game is impossible to make without referencing to the original one, and truthfully, i don't want anything different. the only difference i wanted was control, which i now have cuz i'm developing it."_ An earlier version of this file demanded original mechanics, recipe trees, creatures and biomes. **That was wrong and was actively harmful** — it put weeks of unwanted design work in front of a solo developer who wanted to build the game, not redesign the genre.

  **The originality requirement is retired, assets included.** Ruling 2026-08-17: _"legalities aren't my concern here, my repo is private and the game won't be shipped for playing, it'll just be for personal use, so screw it if i just use mojang assets and never have my friend author them."_ Mojang's textures and sounds are this game's permanent art. Nothing is waiting on a friend to draw replacements, and no future build swaps them out — do not plan around either.

  **So never author art yourself.** The reference art *is* the art: `tools/make-reference-blocks.ps1` stages Mojang's real files into `blocks-reference/` beside each exe and the game prefers them whenever they exist, so **adding anything visible is one row in that script** — plus the cheapest flat-colour placeholder under `assets/`, which still needs a file per layer or the load fails. A session was spent hand-drawing food sprites in ignorance of this; `ASSETS-REFERENCE.md` is the full map.

  **Names still split in two, but now as the user's taste rather than as law.** Ordinary words — *sheep*, *cow*, *pig*, *stone*, *bread* — stay plain English; coined ones — *Creeper*, *Enderman*, *Ghast*, *Blaze*, *Redstone* — stay ours because he prefers it, not because anything forces it. Direct correction, 2026-08-01: _"sheep will still be called sheep right? i'm not compromising there thats not copy-rightable you can't copyright a sheep."_

  So **"how does Minecraft do it?" is a good question for design as well as engineering.** Ask the user where they want something to differ; never invent divergence for its own sake. Where the project should genuinely exceed the original is *engineering* — the renderer, the threading, the absence of stutter.
- **`engine/` must not know that `game/` exists.** The engine is a library; the game is an executable that uses it. If engine code ever needs to reference a game concept (blocks, chunks, the player), that is a signal the abstraction is in the wrong place — the engine should expose a mechanism and let the game supply the policy. This one rule is what makes it possible to eventually have tools/editors/servers reusing the same engine.
- **Prefer plain data and explicit ownership over inheritance hierarchies.** No `GameObject` base class, no virtual-everything. The moment this becomes a deep class tree, both multithreading and cache performance become impossible to recover.
- **Structure for future multithreading without doing it now.** This is the _only_ concession being made to future threading, and it is non-negotiable from the first chunk milestone (`TIMELINE.md` M4) onward, because it cannot be retrofitted:
  1. **Chunk generation is a pure function of `(seed, chunkCoord)`** — no neighbour reads, no global mutable state, no wall-clock time.
  2. **Meshing is a pure function of `(blocks, neighbour borders)` returning vertex data** — it does not upload to the GPU and does not mutate what it reads.
  3. **Exactly one owner mutates the world**, on the main thread. Workers get copies and return results.

  Threads are the easy part; untangling shared mutable state afterwards is the rewrite. This is also the specific weakness the user wants this engine to beat.
- **The renderer was rewritten at M23, as planned, and is now concrete rather than throwaway.** That was never a failure of the first one — building a deferred HDR pipeline before a single block was on screen would have meant carrying huge complexity, blind, with nothing real to measure against. What survived the rewrite untouched was exactly what was meant to: world data, generation, meshing inputs, persistence, physics and gameplay. Only the vertex format churned, and that churn stayed inside meshing. **Do not now add an `IRenderBackend`, a material abstraction or a render-graph layer.** There is still one backend, the seven passes are concrete on purpose, and the same rule applies as before: no abstraction without a second implementation in sight.
- **Rendering resources are owned by RAII types.** Vulkan requires explicit destruction of nearly everything, in the right order. Tying each Vulkan handle to a C++ object that destroys it in its destructor is what prevents this from becoming a leak-hunting nightmare at scale.
- **No abstraction without a second implementation in sight.** Do not write a `IRenderBackend` interface "in case we add DirectX." One backend, concrete, until a second one is actually being written.
- **One milestone, one working build.** Never leave the repository in a state that does not compile and run.

### Coding Habits That Make Later Migration Cheap

User instruction, 2026-07-30: _"coding with multi-threading and graphics and stuff in mind make it easier in the future to migrate to the big guns and you have to think less and i have to worry less about screw ups. time is also saved."_ This is correct, and it is about **how code is shaped**, not about building the future systems early. Apply these by default, in every milestone, without being asked.

**Data and ownership — these make M12 (threading) nearly free:**

- **No global mutable state, no singletons.** Anything a worker might touch should be passed in, not reached for. This one habit prevents most threading rewrites.
- **Separate "compute the result" from "apply the result."** A function that calculates a mesh, a generation result, or a physics resolution should return it, not install it. The caller applies it. This is what makes work movable to another thread later.
- **Explicit single ownership.** Prefer a clear owner plus plain references over `shared_ptr` for hot data. Shared ownership makes it genuinely unclear who may mutate what, which is exactly the ambiguity that becomes a data race.
- **Plain data in contiguous arrays**, not graphs of small heap objects pointing at each other. Good for the CPU cache now, and a prerequisite for handing slices of work to threads later.
- **Keep allocation out of hot loops.** Reuse buffers. This matters for frame pacing long before it matters for threads.
- **If you find yourself wanting a mutex, the design is probably wrong.** Prefer giving a worker its own copy and taking a result back.

**Rendering — these make M23 (PBR/deferred) a contained rewrite instead of a sprawling one:**

- **Mesh generation never touches the GPU.** Meshing produces vertex data; a separate step uploads it. Needed for threading anyway, and it means changing the vertex format later touches two places, not twenty.
- **Vertex layouts live in one place**, not duplicated between shader, mesher, and pipeline setup. They *will* change at M14 and M23.
- **No Vulkan types in gameplay code.** Game logic says "draw this chunk," never `VkCommandBuffer`.
- **Think in batches, not individual draws.** Even while drawing one thing, do not bake in assumptions like one-texture-per-draw or one-draw-per-chunk that a batched or indirect renderer would have to unpick.
- **RAII for every GPU resource**, destroyed in reverse creation order.

**And the counterweight — what "thinking ahead" must NOT become:**

Do not add interfaces, virtual base classes, "manager" objects, template generality, event buses, or configuration hooks for systems that do not exist yet. Speculative structure is not foresight; it is weight that every later milestone has to carry, and it is the single most common way ambitious engine projects die. The habits above are free because they are about *shape*. Abstractions are not free, and they wait until there is a second real case.

## Update Discipline

This file holds **hard rules, working style and architecture** - the things worth re-reading
on every task. Nothing else belongs in it, because everything in it is paid for on every turn:

- A mistake and what it cost → `LESSONS.md`
- How to measure something without lying to yourself → `MEASURING.md`
- Why a choice was made, or why the obvious alternative was rejected → `DECISIONS.md`
- What the code does now, a constant, a command → `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md`
- What shipped when → `TIMELINE.md`

Update existing bullets in place rather than appending a chronological diary. Do not log
routine work - if a change would be obvious to anyone reading the code, it does not belong in
any of them. **Promote a lesson into this file's opening box only when it has cost time more
than once**; that box is the one thing every session reads, and its value is that it is short.

⚠️ **The corpus was measured for repetition on 2026-08-19, so nobody needs to hunt for it
again.** Across **17 documents and 5,448 paragraphs: ZERO exact duplicate paragraphs**, and of
**65,487 twelve-word shingles only 91 (0.14%) appear in more than one file** - most of them the
*generated* index header, a handful of deliberately re-quoted user rulings, and about six
technical passages shared between `TIMELINE.md` and `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` where a milestone entry
explains the mechanism it built. **That last set was left alone on purpose: a history entry has
to read on its own.** The detector was controlled both ways - a planted duplicate was detected,
and the corpus size was printed rather than only the hit count.

**So do not "clean up repetition" on instinct here; there is almost none, and the discipline
above is why.** What these documents accumulate instead is **stale claims** - a note that was
true when written and quietly stopped being true. That is the real maintenance debt, it is
invisible to a duplicate hunt, and `MEASURING.md` §4 is how to find it.
